planting.note: Direct sow after last frost for a summer crop, or sow again in mid-summer for harvest in early autumn once nights cool down; Rondo forms its bulb quickly and holds well without splitting.

directions: Direct sow shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear. Rondo is a modern F1 Florence fennel bred for a fast, even bulbing habit, producing rounded, uniform white bulbs that stay tight and resist splitting even under less-than-ideal watering. It shows notably strong bolt resistance compared to older open-pollinated bulbing fennels, which lets gardeners get a reliable crop from both spring and late-summer sowings. Hill soil slightly around the swelling bulb base as it develops to keep the flesh blanched, pale, and tender. Harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball by cutting at the base, leaving roots in place to often resprout a smaller secondary harvest of feathery fronds.
sources: Chiltern Seeds — Florence Fennel Rondo F1 variety documentation
RHS Plant Finder — Foeniculum vulgare var. azoricum Rondo

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed in spring, or sow again in mid- to late summer for a fall bulb crop, since this open-pollinated selection still bolts if stressed by an early cold spell.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to final spacing, since fennel taproots resent disturbance. Perfection is a long-standing open-pollinated bulbing fennel prized for producing some of the largest, most uniform bulbs among non-hybrid Florence types, with crisp white flesh and a clean, sweet anise flavor. It is often grown as a reliable, seed-saveable alternative to F1 hybrids like Zefa Fino where growers want to select and replant their own seed year to year. Mound soil around the base of the swelling bulb as it enlarges to keep it pale and tender rather than green and fibrous. Harvest by cutting the bulb at soil level once it reaches a good hand-sized girth, before the center begins to push up a flower stalk.
sources: Restoration Seeds — Perfection fennel variety documentation
Wood Prairie Family Farm — organic Perfection fennel seed catalog

planting.note: Direct sow after the last frost for a summer harvest, or sow in mid-summer for a fall crop, since Amigo holds in the field without bolting longer than older bulbing types.

directions: Direct sow shallowly into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin to final spacing rather than transplanting, since fennel seedlings dislike root disturbance. Amigo is an F1 bulbing fennel that produces flattened, broad white bulbs with dense, crisp flesh and reliably resists the premature bolting that ruins many Florence fennel plantings in variable weather. Its flattened bulb shape and tight leaf base make it well suited to close spacing and mechanical harvest in market-garden rows. Hill soil around the developing bulb to keep it blanched and tender, and harvest once the bulb reaches full size but before any central flower stalk begins to elongate.
sources: Osborne Quality Seeds — F1 fennel variety catalog
Epic Gardening — How to Plant, Grow, and Care for Fennel

planting.note: Direct sow around the last frost date in a permanent bed, since fennel forms a long taproot and resents transplanting; established plants self-sow readily and return each spring.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun where the plant can remain undisturbed for years, since bronze fennel builds a deep taproot and returns from the crown each spring in mild-winter climates. Smokey is a selected bronze-leaved strain valued for especially rich, smoky copper-purple filigreed foliage that holds its dark coloring through the season better than seed-grown bronze fennel populations, which often fade toward green. The tall plumes of foliage are topped in summer by wide, flat umbels of small yellow flowers that draw enormous numbers of pollinators and serve as a favored host plant for swallowtail butterfly caterpillars. Harvest feathery leaves continuously for a sweet anise flavor in fish and salad dishes, and collect the ripening seed heads in late summer for use as a spice or tea; deadhead some umbels before seed drop if self-sowing is not wanted.
sources: Renee's Garden — Smokey Bronze Fennel variety documentation
Select Seeds — Fennel Smokey Bronze catalog description

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked for a spring crop, or sow in mid- to late summer for an autumn harvest, since Montebianco is bred for strong bolt resistance across variable weather.

directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and thin seedlings to their final spacing, since bulbing fennel does not transplant well once its taproot is established. Montebianco is a heritage Italian bulbing fennel, its name referencing Mont Blanc, selected for producing mid-sized, very round, solid white bulbs that mature somewhat earlier than many other Florence types. It is prized among Italian heirloom growers for holding a tight, crisp bulb shape without the hollowing or splitting that affects some older strains, and for tolerating the changeable summer weather typical of the UK and Ireland better than most open-pollinated fennels. Mound soil around the swelling bulb base as it develops to keep the flesh pale and tender rather than green and woody. Harvest by cutting the bulb at ground level once it has filled out, and use the feathery foliage as a bonus fresh herb.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Fennel Montebianco (Mont Blanc) variety documentation

planting.note: Direct sow a few weeks before the last frost, or succession sow every 2-3 weeks; Ella is bred short and dense enough to also thrive in pots and trays for baby-leaf harvest.

directions: Direct sow thickly into cool, moist soil in full sun, or broadcast into trays or pots for a dedicated cut-and-regrow crop. Ella is a compact, dark-green dill bred specifically for container growing and baby-leaf production, staying shorter and denser than field dill types like Bouquet or Mammoth while still delivering strong, classic dill flavor. Its tight, upright habit lets growers pack more plants into a small footprint and harvest repeated cuttings of tender young foliage before the plants have a chance to bolt. Shear whole plantings back to an inch or two of growth for a quick regrowth cycle, and resow every few weeks through the cool months for a steady supply of fresh dill weed.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Ella Dill variety documentation

planting.note: Direct sow several weeks before the last frost, since dill forms a taproot and does not transplant well; Elephant stays productive longer than fast-bolting types because it delays flowering.

directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so mature plants have room for their tall, sturdy stems. Elephant is a large, late-flowering dill selection that stays in vigorous leaf production noticeably longer than standard varieties before bolting to flower, giving a wider window for harvesting fresh dill weed. Its height and productivity also make it a strong choice for gardeners who want abundant seed heads later in the season for pickling brine and spice use. Because it delays bolting, Elephant tolerates a broader range of sowing dates through spring and early summer without immediately running to seed. Stake or plant in a sheltered spot if wind is a concern, since the tall stems can lean once heavy with seed heads.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Elephant Dill variety documentation
